children.html: Perceived relationship with God moderates the relationship between social comparison and body appreciation
Kristin J. Homana * and Valerie A. Lemmonb
a Psychology, Grove City College, 100 Campus Drive, Grove City, PA 16127, USA; b Psychology, Messiah College, 1 College Ave, Mechanicsburg, PA 17055, USA

Social comparison has been shown to contribute to the negative attitudes that most Western women have towards their bodies. However, minimal research has addressed the relationship between social comparison and body appreciation, which entails holding favourable opinions towards the body, accepting the body along with its deviations from societal beauty ideals, respecting the body by engaging in healthy behaviours, and protecting the body by rejecting unrealistic media appearance ideals. This study tested whether feeling loved and accepted by God would weaken the inverse relationship between social comparison and body appreciation among a sample of 186 female undergraduates. Results showed that frequent body-related comparisons were related to lower body appreciation, but this relationship was conditional upon the quality of women's perceived relationship with God. Results suggest that future research should explore interventions designed to create improved secure attachment relationships between clients and God.
Keywords: body appreciation; social comparison; attachment to God; positive body image

When people are unsure of how they measure up on some attribute, they tend to compare themselves to others. This nearly universal tendency can produce feelings of distress and reduced selfesteem if the observer comes to realise that he or she falls short of others. Many scholars believe that this process plays a role in the normative discontent that characterises Western women's feelings about their bodies because idealised – and often artificially created – images of attractiveness in the media are pervasive. Indeed, frequent appearance-based comparisons have been shown to increase women's body dissatisfaction. However, little is known about factors that might moderate this process. Growing evidence indicates that religion has healthy links with the way women feel about their bodies and it is reasonable to think that feeling loved and accepted by God would buffer the impact of comparing one's body with others. The purpose of the present study was to test whether a perceived warm and secure relationship with God would lessen the impact of social comparison on body appreciation.

According to Social Comparison Theory (Festinger, 1954), humans have a natural tendency to evaluate themselves on a wide range of dimensions. When clear standards are not available, people seek out information about their own standing by comparing themselves to others. This behaviour is so common that it has been described as "a core element of human conduct and

experience" (Suls, Martin, & Wheeler, 2002, p. 159). It appears to be universal, spontaneous, and automatic (Gibbons & Buunk, 1999; Gilbert, Giesler, & Morris, 1995). Indeed, Gilbert et al. have described social comparisons as "natural, effortless, or even inevitable reactions to the behavior of others" (p. 228).

Sociocultural theorists have used social comparison as a way to explain the way that Western women feel about their bodies. People engage in social comparison on dimensions that matter to them, and women are socialised to believe that appearance, including a thin body, is of central importance (Buote, Wilson, Strahan, Gazzola, & Papps, 2011). Because current cultural ideals for women are unrealistic and unattainable for the majority of the population, virtually any comparison with models or celebrities is likely to produce feelings of dissatisfaction (Groesz, Levine, & Murnen, 2002). However, even comparisons with peers have shown a connection with maladaptive attitudes and behaviours (Carey, Donaghue, & Broderick, 2014; Lev-Ari, Baumgarten-Katz, & Zohar, 2014). In general, the idea that making frequent appearance-based comparisons has a negative impact on body image has strong empirical support from correlational, experimental, and meta-analytic studies (Carey et al., 2014; Groesz et al., 2002; Myers & Crowther, 2009; Vartanian & Dey, 2013; Want, 2009). Although most of this research has explored the effects of appearance-based comparisons, there is growing evidence that other types of comparisons, such as food choices or exercise, are also related to impaired body image (Fitzsimmons-Craft, Bardone-Cone, & Harney, 2012; Homan & Lemmon, 2014).

Given the strong evidence that social comparison contributes to negative body image, it is important to consider possible moderators of this relationship. A moderator is a variable that changes the strength or direction of the relationship between two variables, or specifies particular conditions under which a given relationship exists (Karazsia, van Dulmen, Wong, & Crowther, 2013). Several moderators of social comparison have been identified. For example, both sex and pre-existing concerns about appearance have been shown to amplify the effects of social comparison on body dissatisfaction (in regard to sex, the effect of social comparison was greater for women than men; Myers & Crowther, 2009; Want, 2009). A recent study tested the moderating effect of self-compassion, which is defined as an attitude of kindness and understanding towards one's personal struggles and disappointments. The study reported that comparing oneself to others had a diminished relationship with feelings about the body for women who scored high on a measure of self-compassion (Homan & Tylka, 2015).

It is possible that certain aspects of religion might moderate the link between social comparison and body image. In general, there is a healthy relationship between religiosity and feelings about the body (for a review, see Boyatzis & Quinlan, 2008). However, religiosity is multifaceted, so it is often expedient to look at more specific aspects of religiosity. A small but growing body of work has focused on women's perceived relationship with God, and results have been remarkably consistent. Women who feel loved and accepted by God experience reduced levels of sociocultural risk factors for eating disorders (Homan & Boyatzis, 2010), are buffered from exposure to thin-ideal media (Homan, 2012), report higher levels of positive body image (Homan & Cavanaugh, 2013), and engage in body-related comparisons less frequently (Homan & Lemmon, 2014).

The findings linking women's relationship with God to body image have been explained from an attachment perspective. Briefly, attachment refers to a long-lasting, emotional relationship. Originally formulated by Bowlby (1969, 1973), the theory posits that through repeated interactions with significant others, infants and children develop internal working models, or mental representations of the self and others. Beginning in infancy, individuals develop mental models of the self that incorporate beliefs about their lovability and worthiness of care, while also developing mental models of others that reflect their expectations about how emotionally available and responsive significant others will be in times of need. These inner

working models persist into adulthood where they continue to influence self-concept, expectations for others in relationships, and emotional regulation. Importantly, these mental representations become a source of psychological support even in the physical absence of the attachment figure.

Adult attachment is usually conceptualised along two dimensions: anxiety and avoidance (Brennan, Clark, & Shaver, 1998). These two dimensions represent adults' tendencies to either exacerbate or suppress negative emotions when the availability of the attachment figure is in question. People who score high on the anxiety dimension fear rejection and abandonment by the attachment figure. They are uncertain about their own worth, and doubt the attachment figure's acceptance and availability. It is important to note that attachment anxiety is not simply negative affect, but that it captures a unique aspect of the way people respond to important others (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007; Safford, Alloy, Crossfield, Morocco, & Wang, 2004). People who score high on the avoidance dimension are uncomfortable with closeness and dependence on others. They seek emotional independence from important others, and strive for self-reliance. In contrast, people who score low on these dimensions are regarded as securely attached. They are confident that relationship partners will be available when desired or needed, and are confident about their own lovability.

In the past few decades, attachment theory has been extended as a way of understanding people's relationship with God (Granqvist & Kirkpatrick, 2013; Kirkpatrick, 1992, 2005). Religious people often describe their faith in terms of a personal relationship with a deity, and this perceived bond seems to meet the criteria for an attachment relationship. These criteria include seeking and maintaining proximity, viewing the attachment figure as providing a haven of safety in the presence of threat, and using the attachment figure as a secure base (Ainsworth, 1985). Believers seek and maintain proximity through prayer and worship, perceive God as a source of comfort when threatened, and find confidence for life's challenges when they believe that God is with them (Kirkpatrick, 2005). Furthermore, it has been shown that adult attachment to God can be described along the same two dimensions as adult human attachment (Beck & McDonald, 2004).

It is likely that the effects of social comparison on women's feelings about their own bodies are amplified for women with high God attachment anxiety. Specifically, because people who score high on the anxiety dimension doubt their worth and value, they are likely to look to others for self-validation. Consistent with this idea, it has been shown that people with elevated attachment anxiety report low self-esteem that fluctuates in response to interpersonal feedback implying rejection (Hepper & Carnelley, 2011). They frequently seek reassurance regarding their own worth, and engage in frequent social comparison (Shaver, Shachner, & Mikulincer, 2005; Ty & Francis, 2013). They also stake their self-worth in appearance and the approval of others more than people with low attachment anxiety (Park, Crocker, & Mickelson, 2004). Although these findings have been based upon human attachment tendencies, theoretically, attachment to God functions in a similar manner.

The moderating effect of attachment avoidance on social comparison is less clear. From an adult attachment perspective, people with elevated attachment avoidance suppress negative affect and avoid relying on others. They report high self-esteem in regard to abilities and independence (Brennan & Bosson, 1998) and relative to people with high attachment anxiety, do not endorse approval of others or appearance as sources of self-worth (Park et al., 2004). Previous work has shown that God attachment avoidance shows little or no relationship with various aspects of body image or disordered eating (Homan & Boyatzis, 2010; Homan & Cavanaugh, 2013; Homan & Lemmon, 2014); thus, we did not make a prediction about the moderating role of avoidance.
Finally, most of the research on religion and body image has focused on measures of negative body image, such as body dissatisfaction or eating disorder symptoms. This approach makes

sense, and much has been learnt about the generally beneficial contributions of religion to these problems. However, recently, scholars have shown a growing interest in positive body image. Consistent with the broader positive psychology movement, positive body image defines wellbeing as more than the absence of problems. Instead of low levels of body dissatisfaction and the absence of pathological symptoms, positive body image consists of adaptive ways of thinking about the body and behaviours that promote health and well-being. To date, the most comprehensive positive body image construct is body appreciation. Body appreciation is defined as holding favourable opinions towards the body regardless of its appearance, accepting the body along with its deviations from societal beauty ideals, respecting the body by engaging in healthy behaviours, and protecting the body by rejecting unrealistic media appearance ideals (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005). This construct is inversely related to body image disturbance and disordered eating, and positively correlated with a variety of indices of well-being (such as self-esteem, life satisfaction, and optimism). However, it also makes a unique contribution to well-being, above and beyond other existing measures of negative body image, indicating that it represents an aspect of body image distinct from low levels of body dissatisfaction.

Two studies that explored body appreciation are relevant to the present study. First, it has been shown that women with low God attachment anxiety experienced higher rates of body appreciation, even when controlling for attachment to a parent (Homan & Cavanaugh, 2013). The authors explained this finding in the context of the acceptance model of intuitive eating (Avalos & Tylka, 2006), which posits that when women feel unconditionally loved and accepted by another, they are less likely to strive to meet cultural standards of approval. Second, a recent study found that frequency of social comparison was inversely related to body appreciation. Although the relationship between social comparison and body dissatisfaction has been well documented, body appreciation is not simply the absence of body dissatisfaction, and this study was the first to show that frequent body-related comparisons can detract from body appreciation (Homan & Tylka, 2015).

The purpose of the present study was to test the moderating effect of two dimensions of attachment to God on the relationship between social comparison and body appreciation. We used a sample of female undergraduates from two private, Christian colleges. The sample was restricted to women because cultural appearance norms for women have been found to be more rigid, homogenous, and pervasive than those for men, and thus have a greater impact on women's body image (Buote et al., 2011). In addition, the vast majority of research in this area has used female samples. We recruited a religious sample because a recent study found that a substantial proportion of a secular sample reported that they did not have a relationship with God (Homan, 2014). We tested two hypotheses based on the literature and rationale presented above. First, we hypothesised that three types of social comparison (body, eating, and exercise) would show an inverse relationship with body appreciation. Second, we predicted that God attachment anxiety would moderate these inverse relationships such that women who score high on attachment anxiety would experience a greater reduction in body appreciation than women who score low on attachment anxiety. We did not make a prediction about God attachment avoidance.

Participants were female students at two private Christian colleges in the Northeast. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at each college and all participants were treated in accord with the guidelines set by the American Psychological Association. Students were recruited through psychology and wellness courses; they received extra course credit in exchange for their participation. Following informed consent procedures, interested students received a packet of questionnaires which they completed privately and independently.

The final sample consisted of 186 women with a mean age of 19.9 (SD = 2.01) and mean body mass index (BMI) of 22.7 (SD = 3.83). Participants' BMIs reflected the following classifications: 4.3% underweight (BMI less than 18.5), 76.6% normal weight (BMI between 18.5 and 24.9), 16.0% overweight (BMI between 25 and 29.9), and 3.2% obese (BMI of 30 and higher). Most of the participants were White (89.3%) with 3.7% reporting as African-American, 2.7% multiracial, 1.6% Asian-American, 1.6% Latina, and 1.0% Native-American. The breakdown of the sample by self-reported socio-economic status was as follows: 47.1% middle class, 44.4% upper middle class, 7.0% working class, and 1.6% upper class. Most of the sample identified their religious affiliation as Protestant (43.1%) or Christian other (47.9%); 6.9% identified as Roman Catholic and 2.1% reported no religious affiliation. The majority of the participants attended religious services weekly (54.3%) or more than once a week (23.4%); 14.4% attended one to three times a month, 6.4% attended several times a year, and 1.6% attended twice a year or less. Most of the participants identified themselves as "very religious" (55.6%), 30.3% identified as "somewhat religious", 12.4% identified as "extremely religious", and only 1.7% described themselves as "not at all religious".

The 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005) was used to assess participants' acceptance of and appreciation for their bodies. Its items (e.g., "Despite its flaws, I accept my body for what it is") are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Item responses are averaged, with higher scores reflecting greater body appreciation. Among college women, scores on the BAS demonstrated strong internal consistency reliability and 3-week test–retest reliability, a unidimensional factor structure, and positive relationships to appearance evaluation and body esteem (Avalos et al., 2005). The BAS is currently regarded as the most comprehensive measure of positive body image (Menzel & Levine, 2011). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha was .95.

The Attachment to God Inventory (AGI; Beck & McDonald, 2004) was used to assess women's relationship with God. Participants indicated agreement with 26 items using a 7-point scale (1 = disagree strongly, 7 = agree strongly). The 14-item Anxiety subscale taps themes of anxiety about one's relationship with God (e.g., "I often worry about whether God is pleased with me"; "Sometimes I feel that God loves others more than me"). High scores on this subscale reflect an anxious, insecure relationship with God while low scores reflect greater security. The 12-item Avoidance subscale assesses themes involving an unwillingness to draw close to God (e.g., "I just don't feel a deep need to be close to God"; "I believe people should not depend on God for things they should do for themselves"). High scores on this subscale reflect greater avoidance and low scores reflect greater security. The AGI showed good factor structure and construct validity in a multi-sample study (Beck and McDonald, 2004). Cronbach's alpha for the current study was .87 for the Anxiety subscale and .82 for the Avoidance subscale.

The Body, Eating, and Exercise Comparison Orientation Measure (BEECOM; Fitzsimmons-Craft et al., 2012) was used to assess frequency of comparisons along three dimensions relevant to body image. These dimensions comprise three six-item subscales: Body (e.g., "I compare my body shape to that of my peers"), Eating (e.g., "During meals, I compare what I am eating to what

others are eating"), and Exercise (e.g., "When I work out, I compare the intensity of my workout to how hard my friends say they exercised"). The BEECOM has been shown to have internally consistent and reliable scores over a 2-week period among undergraduate students, and factor analysis upheld its three-dimensional structure (Fitzsimmons-Craft et al., 2012). Cronbach's alpha for the current study was .90 for the Body subscale, .89 for the Eating subscale, and .91 for the Exercise subscale.

Participants also completed a demographic questionnaire that included questions regarding their age, height, weight, race, religious affiliation, frequency of attendance at religious services, and self-reported religiosity (1 = not at all religious, 2= somewhat religious, 3= very religious, 4= extremely religious). Self-reported height and weight were converted to BMI using the following formula: (weight × 703)/height2 .

First, the variables to be included in the moderation analyses were examined for violations of normality. Skew and kurtosis for all variables were within recommended limits for regression analyses (that is, less than 3.00 for skew and less than 10.00 for kurtosis; Kline, 2010). Means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations for the study variables are presented in Table 1. As expected, frequency of body, eating, or exercise comparisons were negatively correlated with body appreciation. God attachment anxiety was inversely related to body appreciation and positively correlated with all three forms of social comparison. God attachment avoidance was unrelated to body appreciation and social comparison. Despite this lack of significant association, the avoidance dimension was included in the moderation analysis because most attachment scholars conceptualise adult attachment as a combination of both dimensions (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007). The two attachment dimensions showed a small but significant positive correlation, indicating that they shared about 4% of their variance. Body mass index was inversely related to body appreciation; for this reason, it was included as a covariate in the moderation analysis. Finally, God attachment avoidance (but not anxiety) was significantly correlated with self-rated religiosity. Specifically, women who scored higher on the avoidance measure tended to report lower rates of religiosity. For this reason, self-rated religiosity was also included as a covariate in subsequent analyses.

The PROCESS macro for SPSS was used to test the moderating role of attachment to God (Hayes, 2013). This tool estimates the regression coefficients and associated statistics for a moderation model, as well as the proportion of variance in the criterion variable uniquely attributable to the moderation effects. In this case, each analysis involved two interaction terms that were formed by multiplying frequency of one of the social comparison scores by each of the two attachment to God dimensions. By including these interaction terms in the regression model, the effect of social comparison on body appreciation was free to vary as a function of attachment to God. Body mass index and self-rated religiosity were included as covariates, and all variables (except the criterion variable, body appreciation) were mean centred. Each of the social comparison dimensions (that is, body, eating, and exercise) was tested separately; hence, a total of three moderation analyses were performed. Results are summarised in Table 2.

Body comparison significantly predicted body appreciation in an inverse direction. That is, the more frequently women compared their bodies with those of their peers, the less they tended to endorse positive attitudes towards their own bodies. This study tested two hypotheses: first, that higher frequency of social comparison would be related to lower body appreciation and second, that attachment to God would moderate those relationships. Both hypotheses were confirmed. The more women compared their own bodies, eating choices, and exercise habits with those of their peers, the lower their body appreciation. However, this association was amplified for women who felt unsure about God's love and responsiveness. Conversely, the relationship was weaker for women who felt unconditionally loved and accepted by God. Attachment avoidance also moderated the relationship between exercise comparison and body appreciation, but because attachment anxiety consistently moderated all three forms of social comparison, the following discussion will focus on attachment anxiety.

A secure, warm, and loving relationship with an attachment figure is thought to provide a primary source of a genuinely positive sense of self-worth (Bowlby, 1988). Individuals can find reassurance about their own value and confidence regarding their acceptance through their history of interactions with this figure. Several intriguing studies with human attachment figures have demonstrated that both conscious and unconscious priming of acceptance by

others can increase feelings of self-worth (Baccus, Baldwin, & Packer, 2004; Kumashiro & Sedikides, 2005). These findings may explain the process involved in the present study. Presumably, when women engage in social comparison, they do not consciously think "because God loves me, I'm not affected by the fact that my friend is thinner than me". Instead, in a manner consistent with Baccus et al. (2004) and Kumashiro and Sedikides (2005), it is possible that unconscious representations of God's love and acceptance serve to minimise the tendency to criticise oneself when making comparisons with a superior target. This interpretation is clearly speculative, and an intriguing direction for future research would be to test this proposition experimentally by priming participants' feelings of acceptance by God.

Previous research showed that women who felt loved and accepted by God (that is, they experienced low levels of attachment anxiety) were less likely to engage in social comparison along the same three dimensions that were explored in this study (Homan & Lemmon, 2014). Thus, women with a secure attachment to God not only engage in less frequent social comparison, but when they do make evaluative comparisons, those evaluations have less of an impact. There are numerous processes other than social comparison that contribute to women's well-being (such as internalisation of the thin ideal or staking self-worth in appearance; Overstreet & Quinn, 2012; Thompson & Stice, 2001) and it is likely that secure attachment to God facilitates a myriad of adaptive cognitive and behavioural responses to these factors. Each response (such as lessened impact of body comparisons) may have a small effect on its own, but it is likely that the accumulation of such responses can produce an overall improvement in well-being. Future research should explore more complex models that simultaneously consider multiple factors known to contribute to women's feelings about their bodies, and how attachment to God moderates those factors.

This study found that feeling unconditionally loved and accepted by God helped to preserve women's body appreciation against the challenges of social comparison. As described previously, body appreciation is more than the absence of body dissatisfaction. It entails respect and care for the body, acceptance of the body despite flaws, and cognitive rejection of unrealistic cultural ideals. While therapy often focuses on reducing features of negative body image (including body dissatisfaction and tendencies towards disordered eating), body appreciation represents an ideal towards which female clients and their counsellors might aspire. One way to preserve or promote body appreciation might be to refrain from social comparison, as social comparison has been shown to have detrimental effects on women's feelings about their bodies. However, because social comparison seems to be an automatic – even unconscious – event (Blanton & Stapel, 2008), results of the present study suggest that for religious women, elevating feelings of love and acceptance by God might be another route to protecting body appreciation.

Theoretically, people's attachment tendencies are the result of years of interactions (or perceived interactions) with an attachment figure. Thus, it may be difficult to change the quality of people's attachment to God. Limited research has addressed this issue. To our knowledge, only two studies have attempted to modify clients' attachment to God through a therapeutic intervention. The first was a pilot test of an 8-week eclectic outpatient psychotherapy group designed to improve clients' emotional experience of God (Thomas, Moriarty, Davis, & Anderson, 2011). Post-test results showed that participants reported increases in their images of God as accepting, intimate, and supportive and decreases in their perceptions of God as disapproving, distant, and harsh. They also reported reductions in both God attachment anxiety and avoidance. However, the study did not use a control group and participants originally sought help for self-reported difficulties in their relationships with God, making conclusions about the effectiveness of the intervention ambiguous. Despite these limitations, the study suggests that interventions aimed at improving people's relationship with God are worth further exploration. Another intervention randomly

assigned college students to either a nine-week manualised treatment explicitly designed to improve participants' attachment to God, a Bible study, or a wait list control. Those in both treatment conditions showed improvements in general spiritual outcomes relative to the control group, but there were no significant changes in attachment to God (Rasar, Garzon, Volk, O'Hare, & Moriarty, 2013). Despite the lack of strong findings, additional research in this area is important because attachment to God has been shown to relate to a variety of mental health outcomes. Incorporating therapeutic techniques that improve clients' perceived relationship with God may yield advantageous outcomes.

This study had several limitations. First, our sample comprised young, mostly White, mostly normal weight women from middle to upper-middle class homes. Much of the body image literature has relied on this type of sample, but clearly, generalisation to the broader population is compromised. Furthermore, students were recruited from Christian colleges and most participants reported that they were at least somewhat religious. A recent study showed that many non-religious people do not perceive a relationship with God (Homan, 2014); so, in many ways, this sample was appropriate for the research questions. Yet, it is possible that students who choose to attend Christian institutions differ in a systematic way from religious young people who do not attend such institutions. A second limitation was that the moderation effect sizes were small. However, as described previously, we suspect that feeling loved and accepted by God serves as a subtle but consistent psychological resource that influences women's emotions and behaviours at multiple levels. Secure attachment to God may have a small effect on social comparison, but the sense that God is loving, available and responsive may confer psychological benefits that accumulate to yield better psychological functioning in general. As scholars continue to explore the connections between attachment to God and mental health, this proposition will be tested. Third, we measured attachment to God along two continuous dimensions (anxiety and avoidance), and secure attachment was conceptualised as low levels on these dimensions. Although our measure of attachment to God was modelled directly upon one of the most commonly used measures of human attachment (the Experiences in Close Relationships Questionnaire; Brennan et al., 1998), which also defines secure attachment as low rates on these two dimensions, it is admittedly a weakness to define a construct in terms of the absence of problematic features. Nevertheless, our interpretation of these dimensions is consistent with hundreds of published studies on human attachment (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007; Mikulincer, Shaver, Bar-On, & Sahdra, 2014; Ringer, Buchanan, Olesek, & Lyasker, 2013). Finally, the study used a cross-sectional, correlational design. Based on extensive evidence that social comparison has an adverse causal effect on women's feelings about their bodies (Groesz et al., 2002; Want, 2009), we assumed that frequent social comparison caused a decrease in body appreciation. It is possible that these two constructs are merely correlates (although our results show that their relationship is conditional on God attachment anxiety, regardless of causal direction).

Despite these limitations, this study makes an incremental contribution to the "God in the bod" literature. It is one of only a few studies to explore relationships between religiosity and body appreciation. As clinicians increasingly adopt positive body image – including body appreciation – as the goal for their clients, this type of research may eventually help them design ways to promote or maintain positive body image. These findings are also likely to be of interest to youth group leaders and other clergy, as they highlight the importance of understanding God's love and acceptance in the context of self-esteem and body image. Finally, this study contributes to the growing literature showing that in regard to mental health, attachment to God is one of the most significant aspects of people's religious experience.
